title: Explicit Teaching Isn't Just Common Sense
author: Debbie Thompson
summary: Debbie Thompson takes up the staffroom claim that explicit teaching is merely common sense and argues that it only looks simple because skilled teachers have done the hard work of making it so. She traces its lineage from Engelmann and Bereiter through Rosenshine and Archer, Cognitive Load Theory and the science of learning movement, then shows how English schools adopt it under many names and how senior leaders monitor it through learning walks and deep dives. Two classroom vignettes carry the argument: a science teacher whose clear explanation skipped eight unspoken micro-steps, and a maths teacher who forgot that novices lack the expert's invisible reasoning. She explains why the approach is exhausting, since it demands sequencing, thinking aloud, checking for understanding and waiting. Teachers adapt the framework to their own personalities, and routines that secure attention make the modelling work. Her conclusion is that explicit teaching is a craft of slowing down, breaking things apart and making thinking visible.
points: The 'common sense' view overlooks that explicit teaching is a structured, evidence-based approach built on decades of research from Engelmann to Rosenshine to Cognitive Load Theory.
Experts skip steps that feel obvious to them, so a teacher can explain clearly and still leave novices lost; the fix is to model the hidden thinking as well as the answer.
The I do, We do, You do sequence gave one teacher's students visible confidence after an observer pointed out eight micro-steps he had never voiced.
The method is demanding because it requires sequencing, thinking aloud, accepting visible mistakes and pausing to check understanding across the whole class.
Routines that win attention first, such as 'Class, watch me', are what let modelling work, and teachers can adapt pace and style to their own personalities.
